# VW Passat Estate B5 - Parking brake suddenly slack but cable not broken

If you are working on a VW Passat Estate B5 and find that the handbrake has gone slack despite the cable remaining intact, the issue likely lies within the mechanical linkage rather than the cable itself. The symptoms you describedâwhere one wheel spins freely while the foot brake operates normally, combined with a visual inspection showing the lever at the caliper fully engaged but failing to retractâare classic indicators of an internal piston failure or wear specific to this generation's disc brakes.

When you lift the center console and observe the equalizer (the cross-member that connects both handbrake cables), seeing one side slack immediately isolates the problem to the caliper assembly on that specific axle. The fact that the cable does not appear to be binding is a crucial diagnostic detail. It confirms that the tension mechanism isn't sheared or stretched beyond its limit; instead, the failure is internal to the hydraulic actuation of the parking brake.

The observation that the lever connected to the cable sits in the "fully-on" position upon release suggests the caliper piston is not retracting as it should. In a functional system, releasing the handbrake allows a return spring to pull the piston back slightly or allows the shoe/disc interface to clear enough for the wheel to turn. If the lever remains seated firmly, it implies the parking brake shoes are physically stuck against the disc. This can happen if the piston cannot slide out of its bore due to corrosion, seized guide pins, or a failed internal seal that prevents fluid from returning to the master cylinder when the handbrake is released.

Your suspicion regarding a cam on the wet side of the piston warrants closer inspection, but consider the geometry of the B5's rear caliper assembly carefully. These units often utilize a specific mechanism where the parking brake shoes are actuated by a lever that pushes against the disc surface. If the "cam" or the adjustment mechanism has worn past its service life, it may no longer allow the necessary clearance for retraction. When you previously replaced the brake light switch and noticed a springier feel with higher cable pull capacity, that was likely due to the new switch reducing friction at the pedal travel point or resetting the cable tension slightly. However, that temporary improvement masks the underlying mechanical inability of the caliper to disengage.

To address this without replacing the entire assembly immediately, you can attempt to bench-bench the caliper. Remove the rear wheels and disconnect the hydraulic lines. Apply a penetrating fluid to the back of the piston where it meets the cylinder bore. Allow it to soak for several hours or overnight. If the piston is stuck due to surface rust or dried brake fluid, this may free the mechanism enough to allow you to manipulate the lever manually. Use a specialized tool or a small flathead screwdriver (with extreme caution to avoid damaging the seal) to gently pry the parking brake shoe assembly away from the disc while applying pressure to the release lever.

Once the caliper is freed, inspect the rubber seals on the piston. If the internal seals are torn or hardened, they may be preventing fluid return even if you clear the mechanical obstruction. In cases where the "cam" mechanism is worn beyond repair, replacing the entire rear disc and caliper assembly is often the most cost-effective decision long-term. The trade-off here is between a temporary fix involving seal replacement and cleaning versus the reliability of a new unit. Given the age of B5 models, finding high-quality aftermarket replacements that match the original specifications is critical; low-quality parts may reintroduce binding issues quickly.

Before reinstalling, ensure the parking brake cable adjuster is set correctly. If the cable was under tension when the caliper failed to retract, forcing it back might have overstretched the cable internally or damaged the equalizer linkage further. Always test the handbrake engagement at a low speed before driving to ensure the wheel locks as expected.
